title: Data Center & Networking Daily Briefing
description: AI fabrics and enterprise networking, data center capacity, power and cooling, and AI storage.
readFirst: Covers Oct. 26–Nov. 6. New: NVIDIA said Nov. 5 that in a 100-megawatt comparison a Vera CPU supports more agents per watt than both the fastest and the most efficient x86 CPU it measured. No separate networking-fabric announcement dated Nov. 5–6 was found. Dell's OneFS 9.16 note is on the partners page. The Nov. 4 ballot item remains. Tom's Hardware's Nov. 5 Moonshot note, about leasing Blackwell capacity in Europe, is on the AI page. AMD's data-center revenue note is on the partners page.

items.headline: NVIDIA says Meta will deploy more Vera Rubin racks with Spectrum-X and BlueField-4
items.summary: NVIDIA said Oct. 26 that Meta intends to expand deployment of Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs for what NVIDIA called next-generation AI agents, and that Meta will deploy Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4 for network efficiency and throughput. The same announcement says the companies will consider additional work on OpenShell and on Sentry, which NVIDIA describes as monitoring for agent behavior. NVIDIA also said it will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering. The release frames the infrastructure work as support for Muse and the Muse family of models.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: PsiQuantum showed an eight-port optical switch for GPU networks
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Oct. 30 that PsiQuantum demonstrated an eight-port optical circuit switch for AI data-center GPU networks, built from silicon photonics with no moving parts and no amplifier. Tom's Hardware says lab tests showed a typical insertion loss of 1.2 dB, and that PsiQuantum told Tom's Hardware the figure is fiber to fiber and does not include connector losses. The article says PsiQuantum has a 64-by-64 version taped out and a 72-by-72 underway. Tom's Hardware says the eight-port device is a demonstration, and that PsiQuantum says samples and testing kits have gone to several computing companies, including GPU vendors and hyperscalers.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: a smuggler says banned HBM is reaching China inside cheap processors
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 3, citing The Information, that a memory smuggler described moving export-controlled high-bandwidth memory from South Korea into China. Tom's Hardware said the person owns a chip-design firm that builds cheap, low-performing processors covered by U.S. and South Korean export controls, then pairs them with high-bandwidth memory from Samsung and SK hynix that would be banned on its own. It said the export rules, as Tom's Hardware describes them, look at the server processor's performance and not at the other components attached to it.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Altman met Samsung on Oct. 30 about memory for AI data centers
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 1, citing Bloomberg, that OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman met about 50 senior Samsung executives on Oct. 30 at Samsung's Resources Development Center in Yongin. Samsung Korea said the discussion covered the direction of AI technology and new business opportunities, and Tom's Hardware says Samsung emphasized AI transformation rather than announcing a new memory supply agreement. Tom's Hardware says Samsung described the talks as strengthening an existing letter of intent to cooperate on global AI infrastructure, including memory semiconductors for OpenAI's Stargate project. Citing Counterpoint Research, Tom's Hardware says Samsung and SK Hynix accounted for about 83 percent of high-bandwidth memory revenue.

items.headline: The Verge: 33 of 45 local ballot measures will restrict data centers
items.summary: The Verge reported Nov. 4 that data-center developers face a more restrictive building environment after the midterms. It said an NBC News Election Day poll found 76 percent of voters opposed data centers in their communities, and that voters faced 45 local ballot measures. As of Wednesday morning, The Verge said, a Redbud Consulting compilation showed that 33 of those results will restrict data-center development. It said Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, several Ohio cities voted to ban data centers over 25 megawatts, and El Dorado, Kansas, voted to ban data centers with a peak electrical load over 10 megawatts for 10 years.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Intel expects the Fab 28 shutdown to cost about $600 million
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Oct. 30 that an explosion earlier this month at Intel's Fab 28 near Kiryat Gat, Israel, killed two people, seriously injured one, and shut the facility for about two weeks. Intel chief financial officer Dave Zinsner said on the earnings call that the site had been shut down for about two weeks and that Intel expected to start production again by the end of this week. Tom's Hardware says Intel expects about $300 million less revenue in the fourth quarter of 2026 and a similar impact in the first quarter of 2027, about $600 million across the two quarters, plus about a 2 percent cut to fourth-quarter non-GAAP gross margin. It says the disruption affects server processors made on Intel's 10nm-class processes, including Intel 7, and that Intel has not named the Xeon families affected or said when the fab will return to full capacity.

items.headline: NVIDIA says Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs are generally available on Oracle Cloud
items.summary: NVIDIA said Oct. 27 that Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are generally available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and that the companies plan to expand OCI Superclusters with Vera Rubin NVL72 to multi-gigawatt scale. NVIDIA said those superclusters combine NVL72 racks, Oracle Acceleron networking with Spectrum-X Ethernet using Spectrum-6 switches and BlueField-4 DPUs, and gigawatt-class power and cooling, and that each rack connects 72 GPUs with NVLink. OCI also plans an HGX Rubin NVL8 with eight Rubin GPUs, two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4 TB of DDR5 memory, and 6.4 Tbps of RDMA networking. NVIDIA said OpenAI has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 Blackwell GPUs in Abilene, and that OpenAI is bringing Vera CPUs on OCI into production for agentic sandbox workloads.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: a local Vera server more than doubled Stream bandwidth versus dual Xeon 6
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Oct. 28 that Nvidia and Oracle have made Vera Rubin NVL72 and standalone Vera CPUs generally available on OCI Superclusters. In tests on a local Vera server, not on OCI, Tom's Hardware said Stream triad bandwidth was more than double that of a dual Intel Xeon 6980P system using MRDIMMs at 8,800 MT/s, and it cited Nvidia's figure of 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Tom's Hardware said Oracle will also offer an HGX NVL8 with eight Rubin GPUs on a dual 64-core Intel Xeon 6 host with 4 TB of DDR5. The outlet said these tests are part of a larger review it has not yet published.

items.headline: NVIDIA says one Vera CPU beats the fastest and the most efficient x86 CPU it measured
items.summary: NVIDIA said Nov. 5 that, in a 100-megawatt data-center comparison, a single Vera CPU performs better than both the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. NVIDIA said Vera delivers 1.6 times more agents per watt than the fastest x86 CPU at what it called industry-leading agent speed, and twice the agent speed of the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. NVIDIA said Perplexity ran agentic coding tasks 1.5 times faster on Vera than on traditional CPUs and plans to deploy Vera in a production system, and that Daytona brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds on Vera versus 88.4 seconds on x86. NVIDIA said the comparison is about running more agents inside a power limit, because agent steps move between GPU reasoning and CPU execution.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: xAI is powering a Mississippi data center with eight jet turbines
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 3 that Elon Musk's xAI is using eight converted jet-engine turbines to power a Mississippi data center. Tom's Hardware said the generators have state-level permission, and that the permits allow a 25 percent higher limit for volatile organic compounds. It said those compounds, together with carbon monoxide, have drawn warnings from environmentalists, and that The New York Times reports the Southern Environmental Law Center has challenged Mississippi's decision to approve the turbines.

items.headline: OpenAI's Grid Protectors plan includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand in Georgia
items.summary: OpenAI said Nov. 2 it is launching the Grid Protectors Program so future compute campuses can reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain, with the amount, speed, and duration set in agreements with utilities. OpenAI said its planned Effingham County, Georgia, campus will pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project, and that its agreement with Georgia Power includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, which OpenAI said equals the average demand of roughly 700,000 households. OpenAI said Georgia Power projects about $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029 from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia, and estimates at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours. OpenAI said the campus is still in development and is intended as a pilot for the program.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Fujifilm will spend 10 billion yen to raise tape output for AI storage
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Oct. 29, citing Nikkei Asia, that Fujifilm plans to raise magnetic-tape production by as much as five times because of AI data-center demand. Tom's Hardware says Fujifilm will spend 10 billion yen ($63.3 million) to increase capacity at its Odawara plant through fiscal 2028, and that the expansion is the company's largest tape investment in about 20 years. It says the added capacity is meant to produce tapes of up to 100 TB each. Tom's Hardware says magnetic tape is used for long-term backup of data that is rarely accessed, and that Fujifilm is one of several storage vendors expanding for AI data centers.
